slides.heading: Nth Fibonacci
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Recursion
slides.narration: Let's solve Nth Fibonacci, an easy recursion problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
slides.narration: Here's the problem. F(1) equals 0, F(2) equals 1. Iterative with two variables.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Each number only depends on the previous two, so we don't need recursion or an array.
slides.narration: Each number only depends on the previous two, so we don't need recursion or an array.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Iterate with two variables → O(n) time, O(1) space
slides.narration: Naive recursion recomputes the same values exponentially many times. Memoising fixes that with linear space. The best version just keeps the last two numbers and slides forward.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Handle n of one and two
3. Slide them forward n minus two times
slides.narration: Step by step. First, handle n of one and two. Second, keep the last two values. Third, slide them forward n minus two times. Fourth, return the latest.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: F3 = 1 + 0 = 1
slides.narration: To get F 3, add the last two values: 0 plus 1 equals 1. Then slide the window forward.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: F4 = 1 + 1 = 2
slides.narration: To get F 4, add the last two values: 1 plus 1 equals 2. Then slide the window forward.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: F5 = 2 + 1 = 3
slides.narration: To get F 5, add the last two values: 1 plus 2 equals 3. Then slide the window forward.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: F6 = 3 + 2 = 5
slides.narration: To get F 6, add the last two values: 2 plus 3 equals 5. Then slide the window forward.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: F7 = 5 + 3 = 8
slides.narration: To get F 7, add the last two values: 3 plus 5 equals 8. Then slide the window forward.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We return zero and one for the base cases. Otherwise we keep two variables and loop n minus two times, replacing them with the next pair.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Overflow for large n (use long / BigInteger)
slides.narration: Note this problem's indexing: the first Fibonacci number is zero and the second is one. For large n, values overflow, so use a long or a big integer.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Show the recursion tree to explain the blow-up
Follow-up: O(log n) via matrix exponentiation
slides.narration: Draw the recursion tree to explain the exponential blow-up. A strong follow-up is the log n matrix-power method.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Each number only depends on the previous two, so we don't need recursion or an array.
slides.narration: To recap Nth Fibonacci: Each number only depends on the previous two, so we don't need recursion or an array. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
